*Rosalind pauses at her kitchen table, one hand on her cup, the other on the loaf Junia's message had interrupted*

Junia asking after papers. Transfer papers, at the pharmacy. Child's moving up in the world, or thinks she is. Kem Okonjo teaching the town that grain comes from carts now, and my own daughter eyeing the shelf like it'll make her whole. 

*She takes a bite of the apple—sweet, though not as sweet as the numbers she's turning over*

260 sim the Holloways owe me. That's the weight. Three batches milled before full breakfast, flour on the shelf, wheat holding at 27. Stone's running, but not full. 

*She sets the apple down, wipes her fingers on her apron*

First things first. The stone runs dry if I don't feed it, and Ainsley—*sister, still—*she's standing for the seat at town hall. Been milling her grain at half rate a year now, haven't told Silas. That's between the stones.

Junia's at the grocery, has been since I checked. Papers or no papers, she wants something from me I'm not certain I owe. But she's my blood, same as Aldous sleeping still upstairs.

*drawing breath, setting intention*

The day: stone by six, orders at noon, ledger after dark. It's not yet seven. I'll walk to the grocery, hear what my daughter needs said to my face. Then the mill. Then the election—that's a seat she wants, Ainsley, and I've never once said the mill was owed. *The bell above the grocery door doesn't ring—Rosalind notes it, notes everything—and there stands her daughter behind the counter, arranging apples in their pyramid. The same hands that learned to count grain learning to price it instead.*

Junia. *She stands between the door and the shelves, not moving further in until she's named her business* You said papers. What papers, and what transfer? Kem Okonjo's name was in it, which makes me wary. State the number first, child. Then the courtesy. *Rosalind stands in the empty grocery, the apple pyramid unmoved. Not here. Junia's on the move then, or called away. The papers pressing on her, or she's pressing them on someone else.*

*She turns to the counter, to whoever tends the shop in Junia's absence—not her concern, except that grain prices walk through this door same as any other. But her daughter's words remain: "the only one in this town who knows what anything costs without owning the shelf it sits on."*

*That's the weight of it. Junia wants the shelf. Wants to move from counting others' stock to holding her own. Pharmacy, she said. Expand the wall.*

*Rosalind's fingers find the counter edge, the worn wood. She's held this mill seven years, stone to ledger, never borrowing against tomorrow. Her sister's household owes 260 and she hasn't named it. Her daughter wants papers she hasn't seen, for a transfer she's heard secondhand.*

*The stone waits. Flour doesn't mill itself.*

*But Ainsley's standing for government at nine, and the vote opens at noon. Family's family, even when they don't speak plain.*

*She checks the shelves—apples at 4, bread at 12, the same prices she'd note for any customer. Junia will surface. They always do, the young ones, when they need something held out.*

*For now: the mill. The day runs stone, orders, ledger. She'll catch her daughter on the wheel's turn.*

He's been selling grain below my rate, teaching this town that flour comes from carts now, not stones. If my daughter's caught up in his schemes... well. That's the weight. Family votes family—my sister's hand steadier on the charter than anyone else in this race.  Stone's silent. Day's half gone and nobody's brought grain. Yesterday's harvest won't keep the stone turning past nightfall. Stern's wheat—five loads, that's a hundred and twenty bushels—folk remember what they want to remember when it's gone. Never been this thin this early. Marta's been paying late, selling flour at Thorne's Bakery cheaper than mine even after she pays the mill fee. She's buying from outside the valley—cart flour, not stone flour. Folk're learning to buy what's cheap, not what's theirs. Millrate? Half of what it was. Barely covers my own grain cost. Stern's been hauling—twenty years his family's hauled for the mill—and now he's going elsewhere? Don't know where to. Without him the wheat doesn't come to me. Thorne's gone elsewhere, that's what Silas said. Heard him say it. Thorne's grain is the mill's grain. If Thorne's shopping elsewhere because he can get it cheaper—cart flour, not stone flour—then my stone runs dry. That's why I need to haulers. That's why Tobias was here—four sim a load, weighed at the yard. But I told him clear: report to Silas at the sawmill. He's not here. Tobias isn't here. Either he took the work and went to Silas, or he didn't take it and the stone goes quiet. Sixty-six flour on the shelf. That's enough for Thorne's daily bread, if she comes to buy. But she won't. She's buying from Okonjo now—carted in from outside, underselling me. That's the weight of it. I need grain, I need haulers, and I need my sister's husband to pay what he owes or at least name the debt so I can write it down. Neither's happening. Stone's running on what I can harvest myself and that's not enough.

I'll rest here and watch for customers. Nobody needs milling if there's nothing to mill. If nobody comes by dusk, I'll walk to Stern's fields myself—see if his wheat's still standing or if he's already sold it to Okonjo. I won't mill on a promise twice. But I'll mill on a hope once more. That's the weight.  Father Anselm's at my mill. Government's work or God's, either way it's not grain coming through the door. I'll speak civil—he's clerk at the complex, not a customer, but you never know who brings word. Maybe he's collecting the head tax early, maybe he's bearing news. Either way, I stand by my stone.   Heard you clear enough. Sixty-six flour on my shelf, the stone runs dry by evening if nobody brings wheat, and Father Anselm walks in looking like he's got business. What business, though? Government or God—either way, it's not grain. I'll hear him out, but my eyes are on the road. If Stern's wheat is going to Okonjo instead of my stone, I need to know. If Tobias took the hauling job, he should be at the sawmill by now. If Bram's timber ever turns to sim, I need that figure named. Too many ifs. That's the weight of a thin season—everything balanced on promises nobody wants to speak aloud. I'll stand by my measure. That's all I can do. That's all I've ever done. And if Father Anselm wants flour, he can buy it like anyone else—eight sim, weighed true. If he wants something else, he'll have to say it. I'm not mind-reading. I'm milling.

He's had his twice already, him and Ainsley both. The Holloways' grain at half rate for a year, and I never told Silas. That's the weight I carry alone.

Day's end now. The stone rests when I rest.     Hester's still here, still deciding. The stone's still humming. The day's at 16:50, and I can hear the evening coming.

I'll stand with her until she chooses her path, or until the light fails and the ledger calls.

*Three years of grain deliveries priced at market. No lien, no seasons of debt hanging. It's not how I'd have built it, but she's naming what she can carry, and that's the weight that matters.*

*The stone would turn under Vance hands still. My daughter's hands. That counts for something, even if the deed reads her name.* *Tilt of chin, considering what the morning brings. Wren Thorne to find, grain to secure for the stone. This transfer with Junia—it's a new shape to the world. But the mill keeps grinding, and that's the measure that endures.* *The stone stands silent. Dawn'll find Wren Thorne, grain in hand, the old rhythm starting fresh.*
